lessonTitle: Medical Mycology: Superficial, Subcutaneous and Invasive Fungal Infection

blocks.text: A 14-year-old wrestler has a ring-shaped, scaly red patch on his shoulder that spreads outwards while clearing in the centre; a scraping dissolved in potassium hydroxide shows branching filaments. Months later, a very different patient in intensive care, neutropenic after chemotherapy, has a fever that does not respond to antibiotics and a chest CT with nodules. The same kingdom causes a nuisance in one host and a lethal infection in another.

blocks.markdown: Fungi are **eukaryotes** with a cell wall of **chitin and glucans** and a cell membrane in which the main sterol is **ergosterol**, not cholesterol. These features are the basis for selective antifungal therapy. **Yeasts** are unicellular (for example *Candida*, *Cryptococcus*), **moulds** grow as filaments called hyphae (for example *Aspergillus*, dermatophytes), and **dimorphic fungi** grow as moulds in the environment and as yeasts in tissue at body temperature. Fungal infection is classified by **the tissue involved**.

blocks.caption: Classification of fungal infection by tissue
rows: Outer keratinised layers (stratum corneum, hair, nails) or mucosal surface
Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton): tinea; Malassezia: pityriasis versicolor; Candida: oral and vaginal candidiasis
Scaly itchy skin, nail thickening, white mucosal plaques; usually no deep invasion
Nodules or lymphangitic spread after traumatic inoculation, such as a thorn prick
Blood and deep organs: lung, brain, kidney, liver
Candida bloodstream infection; Aspergillus; Cryptococcus; Pneumocystis jirovecii

blocks.markdown: **Superficial infection.** Dermatophytes digest keratin and so live in skin, hair and nails; the host response is inflammatory but the fungus does not invade living tissue. They cause **tinea** (ringworm) at different sites. *Candida albicans* is part of the normal mucosal flora and causes **mucosal candidiasis** (oral thrush, vulvovaginitis) when flora is disturbed or immunity is reduced. Diagnosis uses microscopy of a scraping with potassium hydroxide, which dissolves keratin and leaves fungal elements visible, and culture.

**Subcutaneous infection** results from traumatic implantation of fungus from soil or plants; it spreads slowly along lymphatics or through the deep skin and rarely disseminates in healthy hosts. **Invasive infection** occurs when fungi reach the bloodstream or deep organs, almost always in patients with impaired defences. It carries a high mortality, and delay in treatment worsens outcome.

blocks.title: Classifying by tissue
blocks.prompt: Classify each: (a) scaly ring-shaped plaque on skin with fungal filaments on KOH preparation; (b) nodules tracking up the arm after a rose thorn injury; (c) candidaemia in a patient with a central line.

steps.text: (a) The fungus is limited to keratin of the epidermis: a superficial infection (tinea, a dermatophyte).
(b) Traumatic implantation into dermis and subcutis with lymphatic spread: a subcutaneous infection (for example sporotrichosis).
(c) Organisms in the blood with potential seeding of deep organs: an invasive infection.

blocks.markdown: **Who is at risk of invasive disease?** *Invasive candidiasis* arises when *Candida* from the gut or skin enters the bloodstream. Risk groups: patients with **central venous catheters**, those given **broad-spectrum antibiotics** (which remove competing bacteria and allow *Candida* overgrowth), parenteral nutrition, major abdominal surgery or gut perforation, prolonged intensive-care stay, neutropenia and diabetes. *Invasive aspergillosis* follows inhalation of *Aspergillus* spores (airborne conidia), and affects patients with **prolonged neutropenia** (haematological malignancy, stem cell or solid-organ transplantation), those on **high-dose corticosteroids** or other strong immunosuppression, and people with chronic lung disease or cavities (where an aspergilloma may form). *Cryptococcus* and *Pneumocystis jirovecii* are important in advanced HIV infection.

blocks.caption: Risk factors for the two major invasive infections
rows: Gut or skin flora via catheter or damaged mucosa
Central lines, broad-spectrum antibiotics, parenteral nutrition, abdominal surgery, intensive care, neutropenia
Prolonged neutropenia, transplant recipients, high-dose corticosteroids, chronic lung disease

blocks.markdown: **Antifungals.** Because fungal and human cells are both eukaryotic, selective targets are fewer. **Azoles** (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole) inhibit the fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme **lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase**, blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol; the membrane becomes depleted of ergosterol and accumulates toxic sterols, which inhibits growth (largely fungistatic against yeasts). Because azoles also inhibit human cytochrome P450 enzymes to some degree, they have many **drug interactions**. **Polyenes** (amphotericin B, nystatin) **bind ergosterol** in the fungal membrane and form pores, so ions and small molecules leak and the cell dies (fungicidal); amphotericin B also binds cholesterol weakly, which explains toxicity such as nephrotoxicity. Other classes: **echinocandins** inhibit beta-glucan synthase in the cell wall, and **terbinafine** inhibits squalene epoxidase.

blocks.title: Predicting an antifungal effect
blocks.prompt: Explain why an azole blocks growth of Candida and why a polyene kills it more rapidly.

steps.text: Azole: inhibits lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, so ergosterol cannot be made. Membrane integrity and function fail progressively, halting growth (fungistatic).
Polyene: binds existing ergosterol and forms membrane pores, causing immediate leakage and cell death (fungicidal).

blocks.answer: Azoles block ergosterol synthesis; polyenes bind ergosterol directly and punch holes in the membrane.

blocks.caption: Number needed to treat: ARR is the absolute risk reduction (as a proportion) in a trial

items: Superficial: keratin and mucosa; dermatophytes, Malassezia, mucosal Candida.
Invasive: blood and organs; Candida, Aspergillus, Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis.
Polyenes: bind ergosterol and form pores.

blocks.title: Host defence decides the category
blocks.text: The same organism, such as Candida, causes harmless thrush in one patient and fatal bloodstream infection in another. The risk is set by neutropenia, devices, antibiotics and immunosuppression.

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.text: Fungi are eukaryotes, so antifungals are more toxic than most antibacterials; azole interactions through cytochrome P450 matter. Do not confuse dermatophytes (keratin only) with invasive moulds.

points: Fungal infection is classified by tissue: superficial, subcutaneous or invasive.
Invasive candidiasis and aspergillosis occur in patients with devices, broad-spectrum antibiotics, neutropenia, transplantation or high-dose steroids.
Azoles inhibit lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (ergosterol synthesis); polyenes bind ergosterol and form membrane pores.

questions.stem: Which fungal cell membrane component is the target of both azoles (indirectly) and polyenes (directly)?

options.text: Ergosterol
Cholesterol
Peptidoglycan
Mycolic acid

distractorRationale.b: Cholesterol is the human membrane sterol.

questions.explanation: Fungal membranes contain ergosterol. Azoles block its synthesis and polyenes bind it directly to form pores.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman develops itchy, scaly nails and a peeling rash between her toes. KOH preparation of a scraping shows fungal filaments. Which category best describes this infection?

options.text: Superficial: dermatophyte infection confined to keratinised tissue
Subcutaneous: traumatic implantation into the dermis
Invasive: bloodstream infection
Systemic: infection of the central nervous system

questions.correctOptionText: Superficial: dermatophyte infection confined to keratinised tissue

distractorRationale.b: There was no history of traumatic implantation and disease is epidermal.

questions.explanation: Dermatophytes live on keratin in skin, hair and nails, and do not invade living tissue. KOH dissolves keratin so fungal hyphae can be seen.

questions.stem: Which patient is at greatest risk of invasive aspergillosis?

options.text: A solid-organ transplant recipient taking high-dose corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants
A healthy 20-year-old with athlete's foot
A child with a viral cold
A patient on a short course of oral antibiotics for cystitis

questions.correctOptionText: A solid-organ transplant recipient taking high-dose corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants

distractorRationale.b: Athlete's foot is superficial and does not predispose to invasive mould infection.
distractorRationale.c: A viral cold does not usually predispose to aspergillosis.
distractorRationale.d: A short course of antibiotics is not a major risk factor for Aspergillus.

questions.explanation: Phagocyte function is the main defence against inhaled Aspergillus spores, and high-dose corticosteroids and transplant immunosuppression impair it. Prolonged neutropenia is the other classic risk.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man in intensive care after emergency bowel perforation surgery has a central line, parenteral nutrition and has received multiple broad-spectrum antibiotics. He develops fever and blood cultures grow yeast. Which statement best explains his risk?

options.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, a central line and gut breach allow gut-derived Candida to enter the bloodstream
Antibiotics directly cause Candida to mutate into a mould
He has acquired Candida by inhaling airborne spores
Parenteral nutrition kills normal skin flora

questions.correctOptionText: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, a central line and gut breach allow gut-derived Candida to enter the bloodstream

distractorRationale.b: Antibiotics do not convert yeasts into moulds.
distractorRationale.c: Inhaled spores are the route for Aspergillus, not typically Candida.
distractorRationale.d: Parenteral nutrition does not kill skin flora; its risk lies in the central line and nutrient-rich fluid.

questions.explanation: Antibiotics suppress competing bacteria, so Candida overgrows in the gut. A breached gut and an indwelling line give it a route into the blood.

questions.stem: Which statement about amphotericin B is correct?

options.text: It binds ergosterol and forms pores in the fungal membrane
It inhibits lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase
It inhibits beta-glucan synthase in the cell wall
It blocks fungal protein synthesis at the 60S subunit

questions.correctOptionText: It binds ergosterol and forms pores in the fungal membrane

distractorRationale.d: Amphotericin does not act on the ribosome.

questions.explanation: Amphotericin B is a polyene that inserts into membranes by binding ergosterol, causing leakage and cell death. Its weaker binding to cholesterol explains toxicity.

questions.stem: An intensive care unit records 6 cases of Candida bloodstream infection associated with central venous catheters over 4 000 central line-days. Calculate the rate in cases per 1000 central line-days.
questions.explanation: Rate = 6 / 4000 x 1000 = 1.5 per 1000 line-days. Expressing infections per device-days allows units with different numbers of lines and durations to be compared.

questions.stem: In a trial of antifungal prophylaxis in neutropenic patients, invasive fungal infection occurred in 10% of the control group and 4% of the treated group. Calculate the number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one infection, using NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction.
questions.explanation: Absolute risk reduction = 0.10 - 0.04 = 0.06. NNT = 1 / 0.06 = 16.7, so about 17 patients need prophylaxis to prevent one infection.

questions.stem: Differentiate superficial, subcutaneous and invasive fungal infections by the tissue involved, giving one example of each.
markingGuide: Superficial: keratinised layers or mucosal surface only (dermatophytes causing tinea, Malassezia, mucosal Candida)
Subcutaneous: dermis and subcutaneous tissue after traumatic implantation (sporotrichosis, mycetoma)
Invasive: blood and deep organs, usually in impaired host defences (candidaemia, aspergillosis, cryptococcosis)
Superficial rarely causes serious illness; invasive has high mortality
questions.explanation: The classification by depth predicts presentation, diagnosis and prognosis. Superficial disease is a nuisance, while invasive disease is life-threatening.

questions.stem: Describe the groups of patients at risk of invasive candidiasis and of invasive aspergillosis, and explain why each group is vulnerable.
markingGuide: Candidiasis: central venous catheters, parenteral nutrition, broad-spectrum antibiotics, abdominal surgery or perforation, intensive care, neutropenia
Candida is gut and skin flora; antibiotics allow overgrowth and lines or gut breaches allow entry to blood
Aspergillosis: prolonged neutropenia, transplant recipients, high-dose corticosteroids, chronic lung disease
Aspergillus spores are inhaled; neutrophils and macrophages normally clear them, so impaired phagocytes allow invasion
questions.explanation: Candida invades from the host's own flora via breaches, while Aspergillus is inhaled from the environment. Each risk group has a defect that explains the route.

questions.stem: Describe the mechanisms of action of azole and polyene antifungals, and explain why azoles are described as having many drug interactions while amphotericin B is associated with nephrotoxicity.
markingGuide: Azoles inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (cytochrome P450 enzyme), blocking ergosterol synthesis
Membrane depleted of ergosterol and accumulates toxic sterols; growth is inhibited (largely fungistatic)
Polyenes bind ergosterol and form pores, causing leakage and cell death (fungicidal)
Azoles also inhibit human cytochrome P450 enzymes, altering levels of other drugs
Amphotericin binds cholesterol to a lesser degree in human cell membranes, causing toxicity such as renal injury
questions.explanation: Both drug classes depend on the fungal sterol ergosterol but act at different steps. Cross-reactivity with human systems explains their toxicity profiles.
